Stability, controllability and matrix equations

Source: vignettes/analysis.Rmd
analysis.Rmd
library(controlcompR)

Poles and stability

A continuous time model is asymptotically stable when every pole has a negative real part; a discrete time model when every pole lies strictly inside the unit circle. Poles on the boundary need more care: a simple pole on the imaginary axis gives a marginally stable model, but a repeated boundary pole with a nontrivial Jordan block grows without bound. ctrl_stability() distinguishes these cases with a tolerance scaled by the size of A:

ctrl_stability(ctrl_ss(diag(c(-1, -2)), diag(2), diag(2)))$classification
#> [1] "asymptotically stable"
osc <- ctrl_ss(matrix(c(0, 1, -1, 0), 2, byrow = TRUE), c(0, 1), c(1, 0))
ctrl_stability(osc)$classification
#> [1] "marginally stable"
jordan <- ctrl_ss(matrix(c(0, 1, 0, 0), 2, byrow = TRUE), c(0, 1), c(1, 0))
ctrl_stability(jordan)
#> Stability: unstable (continuous time)
#> Poles: 0+0i, 0+0i
#> Boundary poles (within tol = 4.44e-13): 0+0i, 0+0i
#> Stability margin: 0

ctrl_damp() lists natural frequencies and damping ratios (for discrete models through the equivalent continuous poles \log(z)/T):

G <- ctrl_tf(9, c(1, 1.2, 9))
ctrl_damp(G)
#>             pole damping frequency time_constant
#> 1 -0.6+2.939388i     0.2         3      1.666667
#> 2 -0.6-2.939388i     0.2         3      1.666667

Controllability and observability

The rank of the controllability matrix [B, AB, \ldots, A^{n-1}B] is a poor numerical test: its columns grow like powers of A. The package uses an orthogonal staircase reduction instead, which also isolates the uncontrollable modes, and reports the Popov-Belevitch-Hautus test for each eigenvalue so the distance to uncontrollability can be judged:

A <- diag(c(-1, 2))
res <- ctrl_controllability(A, c(1, 0))
res$rank
#> [1] 1
res$uncontrollable_modes
#> [1] 2+0i
res$stabilizable
#> [1] FALSE
res$pbh
#>   eigenvalue pbh_sigma_min controllable
#> 1       2+0i             0        FALSE
#> 2      -1+0i             1         TRUE

A model is stabilizable when every uncontrollable mode is stable and detectable when every unobservable mode is stable. These weaker properties are what LQR, Kalman filtering and MPC need:

ctrl_is_stabilizable(ctrl_ss(A, c(0, 1), diag(2)))
#> [1] TRUE
ctrl_observability(A, C = c(0, 1))$detectable
#> [1] TRUE

Rank decisions use tolerances. A nearly uncontrollable model is reported as controllable with a tiny PBH singular value; the numbers matter more than the yes or no answer:

near <- ctrl_controllability(diag(c(-1, -2)), c(1, 1e-9))
near$controllable
#> [1] TRUE
min(near$pbh$pbh_sigma_min)
#> [1] 7.071068e-10

Lyapunov and Sylvester equations

ctrl_lyap() solves A X + X A^\top + Q = 0 (or A X A^\top - X + Q = 0) with the Bartels-Stewart method on a real Schur form; ctrl_sylvester() solves A X + X B = C. The solution of the Lyapunov equation with Q = BB^\top is the controllability gramian:

sys <- ctrl_ss(matrix(c(-1, 2, 0, -3), 2, byrow = TRUE), c(1, 1), c(1, 0))
Wc <- ctrl_gram(sys, "c")
Wc
#>           [,1]      [,2]
#> [1,] 1.1666667 0.3333333
#> [2,] 0.3333333 0.1666667
#> attr(,"residual")
#> [1] 1.110223e-16
#> attr(,"separation")
#> [1] 1
max(abs(sys$A %*% Wc + Wc %*% t(sys$A) + sys$B %*% t(sys$B)))
#> [1] 2.220446e-16

The solvers check that the equation has a unique solution (no eigenvalue pairs \lambda_i + \lambda_j = 0, or \lambda_i \lambda_j = 1 in discrete time) and report the residual.

Algebraic Riccati equations

ctrl_care() and ctrl_dare() compute the stabilizing solutions of A^\top P + P A - (PB + S) R^{-1} (B^\top P + S^\top) + Q = 0 and its discrete counterpart. The solvers use the extended matrix pencil of size 2n + m, compress the input block with a QR factorization (so R is never inverted) and compute an ordered generalized Schur decomposition with LAPACK dgges. The discrete solver does not need A to be invertible.

ric <- ctrl_care(sys$A, sys$B, diag(2), 1)
ric
#> Continuous algebraic Riccati equation: stabilizing solution
#> P =
#>        [,1]   [,2]
#> [1,] 0.3707 0.1379
#> [2,] 0.1379 0.2354
#> relative residual: 7.45e-16, symmetry error before symmetrization: 4.9e-16
#> closed-loop poles: -2.236+0i, -2.646+0i

The result carries the residual, the symmetry error before symmetrization and the closed-loop poles, so the solution can be checked rather than trusted. When no stabilizing solution exists, for example because a mode on the imaginary axis is not reachable, the solver stops with an explanation instead of returning a wrong matrix:

ctrl_care(osc$A, c(0, 0), diag(2), 1)
#> Error:
#> ! The computed Riccati solution is not stabilizing (closed-loop spectral abscissa 0); the problem is numerically too close to the boundary.
